title: Independent Component Alignment for Multi-Task Learning
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
problem_statement: Direct optimization of an averaged multi-task objective causes optimization instability due to conflicting and dominating gradients, while existing multi-task learning methods converge to arbitrary Pareto-stationary points without mechanisms to enforce user-defined task trade-offs.
domain: Multi-Task Learning — multi-task supervised scene understanding (NYUv2, Cityscapes) and multi-task reinforcement learning (Meta-World MT10)
theoretical_framework: Linear system stability analysis and singular value decomposition (SVD). The condition number kappa(G) = sigma_max / sigma_min of the gradient matrix serves as a stability criterion that jointly measures gradient conflict and gradient dominance. When kappa(G) = 1, the gradient system is orthogonal with equal singular values, which eliminates destabilizing negative gradient interactions. Aligned-MTL provably guarantees linear convergence to a Pareto-stationary solution corresponding to predefined task weights.
methodology: Aligned-MTL resolves gradient conflicts and gradient dominance by aligning the principal components of the gradient matrix G in task space. The algorithm formulates matrix alignment as an orthogonal Procrustes problem min_{G_hat} ||G - G_hat||_F^2 subject to G_hat^T G_hat = sigma^2 I, where the global scale sigma equals the minimum singular value sigma_min(G) > 0. The method computes the eigenvalue decomposition of the T x T task-space Gram matrix M = G^T G = V Lambda V^T, rescales singular values via transformation matrix B = sqrt(lambda_R) V Sigma^{-1} V^T, and multiplies the transformation matrix by predefined task weights w to obtain cumulative gradient G B w. To reduce computational complexity from O(T) to O(1) in encoder-decoder networks, Aligned-MTL-UB aligns gradients with respect to shared representations Z using a chain-rule upper bound.
datasets: Synthetic 2D two-task benchmark with five initialization points
NYUv2 — indoor scene understanding benchmark with 1,449 RGBD images evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction
Cityscapes (three-task) — urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on semantic segmentation, instance segmentation via centroid regression, and disparity estimation
Cityscapes (two-task) — urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation
Meta-World MT10 — multi-task robotic manipulation benchmark comprising 10 distinct manipulation environments

metrics: Synthetic: 2D optimization trajectory plots, cumulative loss landscape, and convergence to Pareto front versus global optimum

NYUv2: Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation; Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation; Mean angle distance, Median angle distance, and percentage within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for surface normals; average per-task performance drop Delta_m_task (%) and metric-weighted drop Delta_m_metric (%) relative to single-task baselines
Cityscapes (three-task): mIoU for semantic segmentation, L1 pixel error for instance segmentation, Mean Squared Error (MSE) for disparity estimation, and Delta_m_task (%)
Cityscapes (two-task): mIoU and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation, Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation, and Delta_m_task (%)
Meta-World MT10: Mean task success rate and standard error of the mean (SEM) over 10 random seeds
baselines: Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA and MGDA-UB)
Multi-Task Soft Actor-Critic (MTL SAC, MTL SAC + Task Encoder, Multi-Headed SAC, Soft Modularization, CARE)
architectures: Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN with SegNet backbone) for NYUv2 and Cityscapes
Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet with dilated ResNet backbone) for NYUv2 and Cityscapes
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron architecture for Meta-World MT10

key_findings: Aligned-MTL achieves provable linear convergence to a Pareto-stationary solution with predefined task weights by enforcing condition number kappa(G_hat) = 1 through singular value alignment (Theorem 1).

On Cityscapes three-task scene understanding with PSPNet, Aligned-MTL achieves Delta_m = -0.02% and Aligned-MTL-UB achieves Delta_m = -0.35%, outperforming single-task baselines and surpassing CAGrad (1.46%), IMTL (3.10%), Nash-MTL (9.38%), and Uniform weighting (14.30%).

On NYUv2 with MTAN across three random seeds, Aligned-MTL achieves the lowest task-weighted performance drop of Delta_m = -8.40% (and metric-weighted Delta_m = -4.93%), and Aligned-MTL-UB achieves task-weighted Delta_m = -7.83%, outperforming Nash-MTL (-7.56%), IMTL (-4.76%), CAGrad (-4.18%), and Uniform weighting (-1.07%).

On NYUv2 with PSPNet across three random seeds, Aligned-MTL achieves the best task-weighted Delta_m = -1.55%, whereas strong single-task PSPNet baselines cause most competing MTL algorithms to suffer performance drops (Uniform 4.72%, GradNorm 2.18%, CAGrad 0.13%).

On Cityscapes two-task scene understanding with MTAN, Aligned-MTL achieves Delta_m = 5.27% (75.77% mIoU, 0.0133 Absolute Error) and Aligned-MTL-UB achieves Delta_m = 6.37%, outperforming Nash-MTL (6.72%), IMTL (11.04%), CAGrad (11.58%), and Uniform weighting (22.60%).

On the Meta-World MT10 robotic manipulation benchmark, Aligned-MTL achieves a 0.97 ± 0.045 average success rate across 10 random seeds, exceeding Nash-MTL (0.91 ± 0.031), CARE (0.84 ± 0.051), CAGrad (0.83 ± 0.045), Soft Modularization (0.73 ± 0.043), PCGrad (0.72 ± 0.022), and shared MTL SAC (0.49 ± 0.073).

Empirical analysis on Cityscapes confirms that the gradient condition number kappa <= 10 reliably indicates training stability and correlates with superior multi-task convergence, whereas gradient magnitude similarity fails to distinguish balanced optimization from severe gradient dominance.
scope_and_delimitations: The authors limit empirical evaluation to multi-task computer vision dense prediction (up to three simultaneous tasks) and simulated robotic manipulation (10 tasks), without evaluating natural language processing or speech domains.
The method requires predefined and fixed task weighting vectors (such as uniform weighting w_i = 1/T) and does not perform dynamic adaptive weight scheduling.
The exact Aligned-MTL algorithm assumes full linear independence of task gradients and requires T backward passes per optimization iteration.

The computationally efficient Aligned-MTL-UB approximation applies theoretically to shared-trunk encoder-decoder architectures, and acts as an empirical heuristic without convergence guarantees for non-encoder-decoder architectures.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: The main limitation of Aligned-MTL is its computational optimization cost which scales linearly with the number of tasks. The upper-bound approximation of the Aligned-MTL method can be efficiently applied for encoder-decoder architectures using the same Jacobian over the shared representation. This approximation reduces instability, yet, it does not eliminate it since the Jacobian cannot be aligned.
limitations.summary: The primary limitation of exact Aligned-MTL is its computational overhead, which requires T backward passes and scales linearly with the number of tasks. Although the upper-bound approximation (Aligned-MTL-UB) reduces time complexity to O(1) for encoder-decoder architectures, the approximation cannot align the shared representation Jacobian and lacks theoretical convergence guarantees when applied to non-encoder-decoder networks.

generalizability_gap: The authors evaluated Aligned-MTL exclusively on multi-task computer vision and simulated robotic control tasks with up to 10 tasks. The authors did not evaluate the approach on natural language processing benchmarks, low-resource code-switched text classification, large language models, or settings with hundreds of heterogeneous tasks.
methodological_gap: Aligned-MTL requires full parameter-level gradient computation across all tasks, which scales linearly with task count; the O(1) upper-bound approximation only aligns gradients with respect to shared representations and cannot align the shared Jacobian directly. Furthermore, the framework relies on fixed task weights and does not incorporate second-order curvature information or dynamic task re-weighting.
future_work: Developing theoretical convergence guarantees for upper-bound gradient alignment on architectures beyond encoder-decoder networks.
Designing methods to align the shared representation Jacobian to eliminate residual optimization instability.
Applying independent component gradient alignment to large-scale natural language processing and multimodal foundation models.
Investigating combinations of principal component gradient alignment with dynamic task weighting and task scheduling strategies.
